pedagogy.summary: Comparing two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator, by reasoning about the SIZE of the parts rather than the size of the digits. Same denominator: the parts are the same size, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same COUNT of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). Both fractions must refer to the same whole. Comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.
bestPractices: Anchor same-numerator reasoning in sharing: the more people share, the smaller each share — 1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 (IES Rec 1).
Reason about part SIZE and count, never the digits alone: 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth'.
Insist both fractions refer to the SAME whole before comparing.
Use fraction strips/bars aligned to one whole and a single number line.
Confront whole-number bias with contrasting cases (3/8 vs 3/4, where the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction).
Read the >/</= symbol as opening toward the larger amount.
keyRepresentations: Aligned fraction strips / bars on one whole
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — a larger denominator means a larger fraction (1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3; 3/8 > 3/4 by comparing denominators) (IES)
Comparing across different wholes (3/4 of a small bar vs 1/2 of a large bar)
Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers
Over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' so blindly it mis-fires on same-denominator pairs

learn.summary: Compare two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator by reasoning about the SIZE and COUNT of the parts, not the size of the digits. Same denominator: parts are equal-sized, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same count of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). When comparing by shaded models, both fractions must be drawn on the SAME whole for the picture to be fair; comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.

activities.title: Lock the numerator, grow the denominator: watch the parts shrink
feedback: If a learner writes 3/8 > 3/4 because 8 > 4, point back to the shaded bars on the same whole: 'You have three pieces on each bar. Which single piece is bigger, an eighth or a fourth? So which set of three covers more?'
If correct, extend: 'If you cut into sixteenths instead, would one piece be bigger or smaller than an eighth? What does that tell you about 3/16 versus 3/8?'
If a learner compares bars of different lengths, stop and insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before deciding.
activities.rationale: Same-numerator reasoning follows from sharing: the more sharers, the smaller each share (1/3 > 1/4). Making the fixed count of parts visibly shrink as the denominator grows directly confronts whole-number bias, a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases.
sourceClaims: Same-numerator comparison follows from sharing (more sharers = smaller share; 1/3 > 1/4); whole-number bias (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3, or 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators) is a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases; children must grasp that a part's size decreases as the denominator increases.
learnerActions: Set up two bars (strips, drawn area models, or an interactive tool) pinned to the SAME whole.
Set both bars to 3/4 to start (numerator 3 and denominator 4 on each), so the two shaded amounts are identical.
On the first bar, raise the denominator from 4 to 8 so it shows 3/8; keep the second at 3/4.
Describe what happens to each part as the bottom number grows from 4 to 8, then state which shaded amount is larger.
Write the correct symbol between them (3/8 __ 3/4) with the sign opening toward the larger amount.
Say aloud: 'Same number of parts (3), but each eighth is smaller than each fourth, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the numerator is held fixed, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller parts, so the fraction gets SMALLER, not bigger. The digits '8 > 4' do not mean '3/8 > 3/4'.

activities.title: Same denominator: count the equal parts
feedback: If a learner reverses this (says 2/6 > 5/6) by over-applying a 'bigger number means smaller' idea carried over from same-numerator pairs, clarify when each rule applies: 'The bottoms are the same here — sixths are sixths. So just count: is five pieces more or less than two?'
If correct, ask them to read the symbol aloud and confirm it opens toward the larger amount.
activities.rationale: Learners who memorise 'bigger denominator means smaller' can blanket-apply it and mis-fire on same-denominator pairs. Pairing this case with the same-numerator case forces attention to WHEN each line of reasoning is valid, rather than to the digits alone.
learnerActions: On one whole, shade 5/6 and 2/6 on aligned bars or on a single 0–1 number line.
State that the sixths are all the same size on both.
Decide which is larger by counting how many equal parts are shaded, then write 5/6 __ 2/6.
Explain: 'Same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two, so 5/6 > 2/6.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is shared, the parts are identical in size, so the fraction with more parts (larger numerator) is larger. This is a DIFFERENT comparison from the same-numerator case and must not be solved by 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Does 3/4 always beat 3/8? The same-whole rule
feedback: If a learner concludes 3/8 > 3/4 from mismatched drawings, ask: 'Were both bars the same size to begin with? Redraw them the same length and look again.'
If correct, challenge: 'Can you make two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction, and show why on equal wholes?'
activities.rationale: Comparing the shaded regions of fractions drawn on different wholes is a distinct misconception from whole-number bias and needs its own explicit confrontation; drawing on a shared whole keeps the picture fair, a precondition stressed in the pedagogy.
learnerActions: Draw 3/4 on a short bar and 3/8 on a long bar, deliberately mismatched.
Compare the shaded regions by eye and notice the drawing can be misleading.
Redraw both fractions on identical wholes and compare again.
State in your own words why, when you compare by shaded pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole for the comparison to be fair.
activities.intendedInsight: When you judge which fraction is larger by looking at shaded regions, both must be drawn on the same whole for the picture to be fair; 3/4 of a small bar can look smaller than 3/8 of a large bar, even though, as numbers, 3/4 > 3/8.

activities.title: Practise and sort comparisons
feedback: Accept an answer only when the learner can justify it by part size or count; a right symbol with a digit-only reason ('8 is bigger') should prompt 'bigger what — bigger number, or bigger piece?'
Mix same-numerator and same-denominator items so learners must select the right reasoning each time, not run one rule blindly.
activities.rationale: Practice and ordering consolidate comparison once part-size reasoning is built; interleaving the two pair types guards against mechanically applying a single rule. Recognition/selection tasks consolidate and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and justification that the modelling activities require.
learnerActions: Decide the correct sign for same-numerator pairs (e.g. 3/8 vs 3/4) and same-denominator pairs (e.g. 5/6 vs 2/6).
Order short sets of same-numerator fractions and, separately, same-denominator fractions from smallest to largest.
Sort pairs into >, =, and < groups and, where used, match a fraction pair to its symbol.
For each answer, state the reason in part-size/count language rather than quoting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in applying the two lines of reasoning across varied pairs, with the correct rule chosen for the structure of each pair.

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support)
feedback: Use this to jog memory, then ask the learner to reconstruct the comparison on their own same-whole model and explain it.
activities.rationale: A fixed fraction wall supports recall of relative sizes but does not let the learner vary a denominator or test a new comparison, so it is a reference scaffold rather than the main investigation.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of a fraction wall, e.g. place 3/8 under 3/4 on the same whole, to see relative sizes.
Use a lift-the-flap or note to recall 'eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4'.
Return to the drawing/building activities to test and justify an actual comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall helps recall relative sizes of common fractions as a reference aid.

constraints: When comparing by shaded models/pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole; a picture drawn on a different-sized whole can mislead. (As numbers, fractions such as 3/4 and 3/8 remain comparable regardless of any drawing.)
Reason about the SIZE and COUNT of parts, never the digits alone (e.g. 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth').
Read > and < as opening toward the larger amount; = means the two amounts are equal.

The same-numerator and same-denominator cases are DIFFERENT comparisons: with a shared denominator compare numerators (more same-size parts is more); with a shared numerator compare part sizes (larger denominator = smaller parts). Do not let a learner apply 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a same-denominator pair.
The fraction wall is a recall aid only; it cannot let the learner vary the denominator or test a comparison, so it should not replace the modelling/building activities.
Recognition and sorting tasks consolidate and check classification but do not on their own elicit independent construction of a model and a justification.
This microtopic targets same-numerator and same-denominator comparisons for age 8–9; general comparison of fractions with different numerators AND denominators is beyond this scope.

Physical fraction strips and card models have slight real thickness and are approximations of ideal equal parts; treat any paper or on-screen model as a model of the same-whole comparison, not the ideal figure itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IES/WWC claim is marked verified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked unverified (verified:false) and is not cited in any activity's sourceClaims.

Interactive examples (two bars pinned to one whole, locking numerators, dragging the denominator, auto-drawn comparison symbol, mismatched-whole warning, tapping fraction-wall rows, lift-the-flap) are preserved as OPTIONAL ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper strips, drawn area models, or a single number line.

Original source rated a third dimension and an in-role conversation as poor-fit for this planar comparison task; these are retained as observations about this task's nature, not as universal claims that such media can never teach fraction comparison.

The original row states the common-whole requirement without qualification; it has been scoped here to comparing represented (shaded) portions, since fractions as numbers remain comparable irrespective of the drawn whole.

The source's whole-number-bias illustration '3/8 > 3/5 because 8 > 5' is retained only inside the cited misconception claim; it is a wrong belief to confront (correctly 3/8 < 3/5), never offered as a valid comparison in a learner task.

probeDeeper: You said 3/8 is smaller. If I cut the whole into even more parts — sixteenths — would one part be bigger or smaller than an eighth?
Which is bigger, 3/4 of this bar or 3/4 of that longer bar? Does 3/4 always beat 3/8?
Write the correct sign between 5/6 and 2/6 — which way does it point, and why?
Make up two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 < 3/4 (same number of parts, but eighths are smaller than fourths, so three eighths is less than three fourths); 5/6 > 2/6 (same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two). Both drawn on the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — '3/8 is bigger than 3/4 because 8 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align both bars on the same whole; show each eighth is smaller than each fourth; use contrasting cases so the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the same-numerator pair by denominator size

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-corrected rule — 'bigger bottom always means smaller', mis-fired so 2/6 beats 5/6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept; clarify WHEN each rule applies — same denominator means compare the numerators (more same-size parts is more)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses or freezes on the same-denominator control set

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across different wholes — draws 3/4 on a small bar and the other on a large bar and compares the shaded regions directly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before any comparison
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses mismatched-size wholes for the two fractions

responseLevels.gap: Orders by comparing digits (denominator or numerator alone); says 3/8 > 3/4; may reverse the same-denominator pair.
responseLevels.full: Writes 3/8 < 3/4 and 5/6 > 2/6, justifies each on a same-whole model by reasoning about part size and count, and recognises the whole must be the same for a fair comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the same-denominator comparison right but falters on the same-numerator pair (whole-number bias), or gets both by a rule without a same-whole model or part-size reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: using bars drawn on the same whole (or a number line), show which is larger and write >, <, or = — first for 3/8 and 3/4, then for 5/6 and 2/6. I'll watch how you build and decide each one.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The same-numerator pair (3/8 vs 3/4) triggers whole-number bias — a child ordering by denominator writes 3/8 > 3/4. The same-denominator control (5/6 vs 2/6) catches a child who has memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and blanket-reverses, wrongly making 2/6 > 5/6. Only part-size reasoning gets both right.
